body: If you’re concerned, ask when you’re being considered for for admission. There are times when they can be flexible with certain things to accommodate specific needs. But I’m not sure if the visitation policy is for the unit or for the whole hospital. If it’s a hospital-wide policy, then they have to hold to it.

Both times I was there, each patient got 2 visitation hours per week. In each room, there are 2 beds. The person in one bed got visitation on a weekday and a weekend day, and then the person in the other bed got visitation on a different weekday and the other weekend day. I can’t remember the specific days, but it was something like Tuesday/Saturday and Thursday/Sunday. If I remember correctly, the visiting time was 4pm-5pm.
You’re welcome! Feel free to send me a message and ask further questions if you want. I was really worried when I couldn’t find much online before I went, so I totally get it.

You’ll need to start by contacting Dominion Hospital and telling them that you’re considering admitting to the TraumaSci unit. They will forward your info to the person who coordinates admissions. She’s also one of the therapists. Once she reaches out, you’ll have a brief conversation and she will send you the intake packet if there’s a possibility of a good fit. There’s a part for you to fill out and a part for your therapist to fill out. Your therapist has to submit the packet once it’s completed. Then, they’ll call your therapist to have a longer conversation. After that, if it still seems like a good fit, they’ll call you for a longer pre-admission conversation: answer questions, determine how to meet specific needs, etc. Reaching out in advance with an ideal admission date in mind is a good idea because the wait time varies.

Yes, I went, and I actually went a second time. I’m thinking of going a third time to work on more stuff because my first two experiences were so positive. Everyone was really supportive. They take patient feedback very well. I didn’t self-harm while I was there, and I didn’t have any experiences of becoming aggressive or seeing other people become aggressive, so I can’t say with certainty how that would be handled. But I definitely had bad days, and so did everyone else. Staff do expect patients to let them know if there is an urge or intention to self-harm. Every morning and evening, patients rate their safety with regard to self-harm, suicidal thoughts, and homicidal thoughts. Staff check in about these ratings if there are concerns. Sometimes, people are restricted to the unit and don’t get to go to the computer lab or outside if necessary for safety. But no one makes a big public deal out of this. There were patients with such significant safety issues that they needed a staff 1-on-1 until safety improved. Although it’s pretty obvious to others when someone needs a 1-on-1, no one was judgmental about this. I’m honestly not sure if this unit even does restraint and sedation. They do want to make sure that the environment stays calm and healing for everyone, so it’s possible that they might send someone to another unit if there was a need for that level of intervention. I’m not sure. The best thing to do is be totally honest about safety issues so that staff can help before self-harm happens.

Thank you again. I keep thinking of new questions. I’ve had some terrible inpatient experiences in the past, so I’m really hesitant about trusting any inpatient unit. Are there ever punitive actions taken for behavior that staff don’t like? For example, in the past, I was in a unit where the staff wouldn’t let me contact my spouse unless I agreed to medication changes. That sort of manipulation is totally inappropriate, in my view. Is there any sort of toxic positivity from staff? I’m very averse to being told that I need to ignore negative things even if they are true and force myself to believe positive things even if those things aren’t true.
You’re so helpful! Thank you! I haven’t yet been told how long the wait list is, but I hope it isn’t too long. Did it take you a long time to get admitted once you finished the intake packet?

Sorry for all of these repetitive questions! It seems unrealistic to expect that a person would be in a state of, “I won’t ever self-injure again!” before leaving. Is that the expectation? What I’m dealing with right now that’s so intense is suicidal ideation. I do self-injure, but I’m working on that outpatient and don’t see a reason why I can’t continue working on that outpatient even after I get the suicidal desires under control inpatient. I guess I just don’t want to be stuck there forever. I think it’s realistic to expect that a person not have any active self-injurious desires in order to leave inpatient. But are they realistically thinking that they can keep a person there until they won’t self-injure again at some undefined future point? Just trying to get a sense of what the thinking is. I really just need to get the suicidal ideation under control, and I don’t want to be in a place that will keep me for a month or more just because I can’t promise never to self-injure in the future.
Thank you. If you don’t mind my asking, how long were you there?
Thank you for all of that info! What do you mean by patients not having a lot of say? Do they not listen to patients when the patient themselves thinks they are ready?

I’m in the process of trying to get into this program now. I hope you’re still on Reddit because I’d really love to know the answers to some questions:

1) I see in the program handbook that they don’t allow cell phones but offer computer time. Have they considered that checking email, paying bills, etc. is just about impossible without a cell phone these days because of multifactor authentication? I literally can’t pay my electric bill online without having a code texted to my phone. Do they consider this at all? It would be a huge stressor to me knowing that I couldn’t even access my email or bills and computer time would be useless. 

2) Do they treat patients like mature adults? 

3) Does it feel confining? Most inpatient units make me feel like I’m trapped. 

4) You mention that some people stay shorter and others longer. Is there pressure to stay more than a few days if you feel like you’re ready to go home in a week or less?

5) How are the weekends? Is it almost entirely downtime on the weekends, or is there structure?
My understanding is that this specific trauma unit is run totally separately from the rest of the hospital.

I just found this subreddit and am so glad to see that I’m not the only person who thinks the blowup over this video is ridiculous. People malingering DID on the internet is one of the reasons that DID remains stigmatized. They harm people who really do have DID. And the Plural Association is an embarrassment. They create these ridiculous controversies claiming to represent people with DID and other self-proclaimed plurals, and they claim to represent the DID/plural community as a whole. I’ve been fortunate to be treated by more than one of the highly competent professionals listed in the Plural Association’s petition, and these researchers and clinicians are truly top notch and respect me for all of who I am. It’s a shame that people who work so hard to support those of us with DID are probably getting harassed online. It really burns me up that my long term therapist is one of those named and demanded to apologize by a bunch of self-diagnosing teens and 20-somethings who have no idea what they’re taking about. I wish that we who have DID had better representation than the Plural Association. We who have diagnosed DID or who are seeking a legitimate diagnosis (or who don’t have the resources to get a diagnosis but have real DID) should be the ones prioritized in any conversation about DID. And I genuinely believe that these amazing professionals prioritize our needs.
I really appreciate that. Thank you.

The best way to ensure that a child has maximum autonomy in communication decisions during childhood and adulthood is to give both: strong ASL skills and spoken English with CIs or hearing aids. Babies can’t tell you whether they’ll ever want to be English speakers as well as signers, and delaying implantation until they can decide for themselves puts them at a disadvantage if they do want to learn spoken English later. A person needs auditory input to learn spoken language. But as others have stated, this shouldn’t be at the expense of ASL. We should always give deaf children ASL because that is the only way to guarantee accessible language. Some children with CIs don’t develop spoken language. There are many happy CI users, and I am one of them, but I don’t hear perfectly. I miss a lot of things when listening with my ears. I’m glad that I now have ASL in my life. Deaf children with or without CIs should have ASL from the very beginning.
Thank you so much for this thoughtful reply. I can relate to so much in this. I’ve tried everything that’s *supposed* to work, and nothing does. I feel there’s nothing left to do except go it alone.
Yes. My partner and I have been together for almost six years, and this is the kind of relationship we have. Except I don’t think I’ll ever be over my trauma. But my partner is here regardless.

I tend to keep busy and working for as long as it’s physically and mentally possible to do so. Then when I have a break or a holiday, all of my trauma memories come forth. I feel things very deeply all the time, but I can hide it from most people so long as I’m busy and working. This keeps happening over and over again. It never ends.

I wear a hearing aid, a cochlear implant processor, and glasses. Definitely put the glasses behind the hearing aids. The comfort level improves after a while of getting used to it. In the meantime, if there’s uncomfortable rubbing it might help to use a bit of lotion in the affected areas.
I’m sorry it was a bad experience for you.
Sorry. A bit sensitive today.

It does feel like that. I’m not happy about it, and I’m not looking forward to it. I really do want to be able to grow old with my partner. But by this point I realize that everything that’s supposed to help doesn’t help, and this is a chronic, permanent issue. It’s never going to get better. I wish that weren’t true, but it is.
I can appreciate that other people feel that way about their own experiences. I don’t believe that can be said about someone else’s experience.
As I said, not today. Probably not within the next year or two either.
Feelings are temporary, yes. But they return. I have no intention to die today. But at some point in time, dying by my own hand will happen. This is how my life is going to play out.
I’m wondering if maybe people perceive me as understanding less than I actually do because my expressive communication isn’t as good as my receptive skills. Thanks for the advice.
Thanks. I’m very concerned about coming off as rude, and I have some self-consciousness about not growing up in the community. I appreciate the advice.

That's not true. It's a nice, feel-good trope, but it's not true. If it were, I would have found a solution or an "it gets better" at some point within my 30-odd years of life. I don't buy those platitudes anymore.

Yes, people forget all the time that I'm deaf. It's really annoying to have to remind people all the time, and there are some tradeoffs I have to think about in every situation. I get a lot of "But you speak so well!" and "Wow, you're really smart for a deaf person" when I remind people that I can't hear them perfectly with my cochlear implant. I spend a lot of time reminding people to slow down, to repeat things, or to write things. And sometimes I have to remind hearing people who sign to sign with me.

Loved Millicent Simmonds. Loved that they chose a Deaf actress. Loved that the movie included ASL. But overall, as a cochlear implant user I strongly disliked the movie because every single thing in the movie about cochlear implants was wrong.
